fetched_contents.text: Benchmarking and Building Performance Standards Policy Toolkit EPA’s Benchmarking and Building Performance Standards Policy Toolkit aims to inform and support state and local government decision makers who are exploring adopting policies focused on reducing energy use and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from existing commercial and multifamily buildings in their communities. As state and local governments establish climate commitments, achieving emission reductions from buildings is critical for reaching decarbonization goals. In the US, commercial and residential buildings account for nearly 40% of energy consumed and over 30% of GHG emissions. Improved performance in existing buildings can help to achieve decarbonization goals and deliver many additional benefits, including: energy cost savings, increased building asset values, local job creation, improvements to indoor air quality, tenant comfort and productivity, and improved air quality from reduced power plant emissions. Benchmarking Benchmarking refers to measuring a building’s energy use (and in some cases water use) and comparing it to the energy use of similar buildings, its own historical usage, or a reference performance level. energy use of buildings is a key first step to understanding and improving energy performance and reducing carbon footprints. Many state and local governments have coupled benchmarking policies with other programs aimed at encouraging building performance, including voluntary campaigns, building energy audits, retrocommissioning, or building performance standards A building performance standard is a policy that requires building owners to meet performance targets by actively improving their buildings over time, often with interim targets that drive energy savings and emissions reductions.. As more state and local governments seek to adopt BPS and other polices for existing buildings, this toolkit can offer: * Key considerations for policy design * Opportunities for cross-jurisdictional coordination * Strategies for using EPA’s ENERGY STAR® Portfolio Manager® tool The toolkit includes four sections focused on different aspects of policy development, each intended to build on the previous section. As BPS policies are new and evolving, EPA will seek to update this toolkit and add new resources, including a resource to help state and local governments identify performance metrics. Toolkit Sections Section 1: Building Energy Benchmarking and Transparency: Overview for State and Local Decision Makers (pdf) (1.6 MB) Provides information about benchmarking and transparency policies, describes key considerations for success, and demonstrates how government leaders have used benchmarking to help enact a BPS. Section 2: Building Performance Standards: Overview for State and Local Decision Makers (pdf) (2.74 MB) Provides an overview of building performance standards and offers information on key decision points to consider when designing a BPS. Section 3: State and Local Government Coordination: Benchmarking and Building Performance Standards (pdf) (1.26 MB) Describes the varied roles that state and local decisions makers have in establishing existing building policies and opportunities to coordinate across jurisdictions. Section 4: Data Access: A Fundamental Element for Benchmarking and Building Energy Performance Policies (pdf) (612.9 KB) Describes the critical role that utilities play in providing whole-building energy consumption data to enable compliance with benchmarking and transparency and BPS polices. Data Access: Sample Policy Language (pdf) (213.61 KB) Fact sheet that offers sample policy language to support utility data access. Data Access: How to Compile and Deliver Aggregate Whole-Building Data (pdf) (266.61 KB) Fact sheet that describes technical considerations that utilities must work through to successfully compile and deliver aggregate whole-building data. External benchmark values are comparison points used in environmental assessments to evaluate how a project, building, or activity performs relative to a standard or reference level. In practice, they help decision-makers judge whether a proposed action is environmentally acceptable, efficient, or aligned with broader sustainability goals [N1-R2]. The EPA’s Benchmarking and Building Performance Standards Policy Toolkit explains that benchmarking refers to measuring a building’s energy use and comparing it to the energy use of similar buildings, its own historical usage, or a reference performance level [N5-F1]. This is a core practical example of how benchmark values are established: by linking a subject to a comparable external standard or baseline [N5-F1].

The attributes typically benchmarked in environmental assessments depend on the context, but building-related benchmarks often focus on energy use, water use, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The EPA toolkit states that many state and local governments couple benchmarking policies with other programs aimed at encouraging building performance, including voluntary campaigns, energy audits, retrocommissioning, and building performance standards. It also notes that energy use of buildings is a key first step to understanding and improving energy performance and reducing carbon footprints [N5-F1]. The toolkit further mentions GHG emissions and energy, water, and waste costs as tracked metrics [N7-R4]. This indicates that external benchmarks commonly cover energy intensity, emissions intensity, and operational resource use, especially in buildings [N5-F1][N7-R4].

Benchmarks matter because they support comparison and decision-making. The benchmark methodology described in the environmental impact assessment literature makes it possible to assess impacts by objective considerations and to conduct comparisons [N1-R2]. In buildings, benchmarking helps governments and jurisdictions identify performance metrics and establish policies that drive energy savings and emissions reductions [N5-F1]. The toolkit also highlights that improved performance in existing buildings can help achieve decarbonization goals and deliver benefits such as energy cost savings, increased building asset values, local job creation, indoor air quality improvements, tenant comfort, productivity, and reduced power plant emissions [N5-F1]. In short, benchmark values turn abstract environmental goals into actionable targets by providing a common reference against which performance can be judged [N1-R2][N5-F1].

Bottom-up approaches generate benchmark values by starting with detailed, site-specific data and aggregating it into a broader estimate. The evidence suggests that bottom-up methods use building-level or element-level data rather than relying on external standards as the starting point. One source notes that bottom-up benchmarks for building elements are calculated following a best-in-class (top 5%) approach, and that a workflow applies these benchmarks [N2-R3]. Another source in the search results refers to generating benchmarks and/or target values based on best practices, with the procedure following a top-down or bottom-up approach [N2-R5]. While this latter excerpt is not fully quoted, it is relevant because it shows that bottom-up benchmarking is positioned as a method of deriving target values from practice-based criteria rather than from a single external standard [N2-R5].

The data sources used in bottom-up methods are typically operational and granular. In building assessments, the EPA toolkit explains that benchmarking is based on measuring a building’s energy use and comparing it to similar buildings, its own historical usage, or a reference performance level [N5-F1]. This implies that bottom-up benchmarking may draw from utility data, energy consumption records, historical usage patterns, and building-specific metrics such as ENERGY STAR scores [N5-F1][N7-R4]. The benchmark dose literature also indicates that benchmark methods can be applied using quantitative and qualitative indicators, with criteria developed for environmental impact assessment [N6-R2]. This reinforces that bottom-up benchmarking is not purely statistical; it often includes indicator selection, verification, and application [N6-R2].

Inputs are aggregated into benchmark estimates by summarizing site-specific data and comparing it against a reference or peer group. In the building context, benchmarking is described as measuring energy use and then comparing it to similar buildings, which effectively aggregates individual building data into a benchmark-level comparison [N5-F1]. The bottom-up workflow described in the design-process paper similarly suggests that detailed building-element data are used to calculate benchmarks [N2-R3]. However, this approach depends on assumptions that the selected data are representative of the population or target group being compared, that the aggregation is statistically valid, and that the chosen reference group is comparable [N2-R3][N2-R5].

Bottom-up benchmarking has several limitations and assumptions. First, it can be data-intensive and dependent on the availability and quality of site-specific records [N5-F1]. Second, it assumes that the benchmark reference group is sufficiently comparable to the subject being assessed; otherwise, the comparison may be misleading [N5-F1][N2-R3]. Third, because it starts with detailed local data, it may be more sensitive to measurement error and less generalizable than top-down methods [N2-R3]. Finally, the use of best-in-class approaches implies an assumption that a small subset of high-performing examples can inform a broader target, which may not always be defensible without additional validation [N2-R3].

Top-down approaches establish benchmark values by deriving them from external datasets, regulatory standards, or broad policy targets rather than from detailed site-specific data. The evidence indicates that top-down benchmarks can be defined based on political or regulatory targets. One source explicitly states that top-down benchmarks are typically defined based on a political target, such as the 2-degree target defined in the Paris Agreement in 2015 [N3-R1]. This shows that top-down benchmarks are often framed by broader environmental or policy goals, which then become the reference point for assessing performance [N3-R1].

The reference datasets or regulatory standards used in top-down benchmarking include environmental regulations, climate targets, and policy frameworks. The Paris Agreement’s 2-degree target is an example of a regulatory-standard-like benchmark that sets an upper limit for temperature rise [N3-R1]. The benchmarking literature also describes a top-down methodology for assessing environmental flows in Australian rivers, which implies that hydrological benchmarks can be established using flow records or regulatory water-quality standards [N3-R2]. In building and energy contexts, the EPA toolkit notes that benchmarking is often linked to building performance standards and that state and local governments may adopt policies aimed at reducing energy use and GHG emissions [N5-F1]. These policies and standards themselves function as external references for benchmarking [N5-F1].

Benchmarks are derived from external data by applying a standard or target to a subject. In the top-down flow-assessment example, the methodology is described as a “top-down” approach for assessing environmental flows, suggesting that a predefined standard or regulatory threshold is applied to determine acceptable environmental conditions [N3-R2]. The Paris Agreement example shows that a global climate target can become the basis for sectoral or project-level benchmarks [N3-R1]. In building performance, benchmarking often compares a building’s energy use to a reference performance level, which may be derived from a standard, policy requirement, or average benchmark [N5-F1]. This means that top-down benchmarks are usually derived by mapping external standards or targets onto the subject’s performance [N3-R1][N3-R2][N5-F1].

Top-down benchmarking has its own limitations and assumptions. One limitation is that it may be less sensitive to site-specific conditions and more susceptible to policy or regulatory shifts [N3-R1]. Another assumption is that the external standard is both meaningful and comparable to the subject being assessed; otherwise, the benchmark may not reflect actual environmental or operational realities [N3-R2][N5-F1]. The methodology also depends on the availability and relevance of the external data source; if the standard is outdated or not well aligned with local conditions, the benchmark may lack practical utility [N3-R1][N3-R2]. Overall, top-down benchmarking is efficient and policy-aligned, but it risks being too generic or detached from local performance details [N3-R1][N3-R2].

Benchmark values are validated and applied in practice through a combination of data quality checks, statistical verification, and policy alignment. The EPA’s Benchmarking and Building Performance Standards Policy Toolkit emphasizes that improved building performance depends on accurate energy data and that utilities play a critical role in providing whole-building energy consumption data to enable compliance with benchmarking and transparency policies [N5-F1]. This implies that validation begins with ensuring data access and quality [N5-F1]. The toolkit also explains that benchmarking is used to track GHG emissions and energy, water, and waste costs, suggesting that benchmark values are validated by repeated measurement and comparison across time and buildings [N7-R4][N5-F1].

Validation methods for benchmark accuracy include checking data completeness, consistency, and representativeness. The EPA’s Benchmark Dose Technical Guidance is relevant here because it provides guidance on applying the benchmark dose approach and determining the point of departure for health effects data [N5-R2]. Although this is health risk assessment rather than building benchmarking, it shows that benchmark methods are often supported by technical guidance that defines acceptable statistical procedures and uncertainty ranges [N5-R2]. The broader benchmarking literature also indicates that quantitative and qualitative indicators are identified and verified in environmental impact assessment, and that criteria are developed and applied [N6-R2]. This suggests that benchmark validation may involve indicator selection, verification, and application checks [N6-R2].

Benchmark values are reported and interpreted as performance indicators relative to a reference level. The EPA toolkit states that benchmarking refers to measuring a building’s energy use and comparing it to the energy use of similar buildings, its own historical usage, or a reference performance level [N5-F1]. It also explains that ENERGY STAR scores indicate a building’s energy performance and that benchmarking helps identify performance metrics [N5-F1][N7-R4]. This means that benchmark values are typically reported as scores, intensity ratios, or relative rankings, and are interpreted as indicators of efficiency, compliance, or improvement potential [N5-F1][N7-R4]. The toolkit further notes that benchmarking can be used in transparency policies, building performance standards, and energy audits, showing that benchmark values are interpreted in policy and compliance contexts rather than as standalone scientific metrics [N5-F1].

Use cases and decision-support roles are widespread. In buildings, benchmarking supports energy reduction, GHG emission reduction, energy cost savings, increased building asset values, local job creation, indoor air quality improvements, tenant comfort, and reduced power plant emissions [N5-F1]. In environmental assessments, benchmark methodology is used to assess impacts by objective considerations and to conduct comparisons [N1-R2]. The benchmark dose guidance also supports risk assessment by helping determine the point of departure for health effects data [N5-R2]. Taken together, benchmark values serve decision-making roles such as setting targets, evaluating performance, enforcing standards, and identifying areas for improvement [N1-R2][N5-F1][N5-R2].

Bottom-up and top-down approaches differ fundamentally in their starting point and scope. Bottom-up methods begin with detailed, local data and aggregate it into a benchmark estimate, while top-down methods derive benchmarks from external standards, policy targets, or broad datasets [N4-R4][N4-R1]. In building environmental assessments, bottom-up approaches often use building-level or element-level data, including utility energy consumption records, historical usage, and reference performance levels [N9]. Top-down approaches, by contrast, may be defined by political targets such as the 2-degree Paris Agreement target or by regulatory standards and flow thresholds [N10].

A key similarity is that both approaches aim to establish a reference against which performance can be measured. The upstream reports show that benchmark values support comparison and decision-making by providing a common standard for judging energy use, emissions, and operational efficiency [N8]. They also both rely on validation and data quality checks in practice [N12]. A difference is that bottom-up methods are more site-specific and data-intensive, while top-down methods are more policy-aligned and broader in scope [N9][N10]. The comparison source also notes that bottom-up estimates account for every known source and a best-guess estimate for each, whereas top-down approaches can be heavily dependent on dataset quality and may differ substantially from bottom-up results [N4-R5].

Each approach is preferred depending on the context. Bottom-up methods are especially useful when detailed local data are available and when the goal is to derive performance-specific benchmarks for individual buildings or building elements [N9]. They are well suited to benchmarking, energy audits, retrocommissioning, and building performance standards because they can map to actual usage patterns and historical benchmarks [N5-F1]. Top-down methods are preferred when there is a strong external standard, policy target, or regulatory benchmark, such as climate targets, water-quality thresholds, or building-performance requirements [N10][N3-R1]. They are especially useful for setting directionality, enforcing compliance, and aligning projects with broader sustainability goals [N8][N10].

The approaches can be reconciled or combined by integrating the strengths of each. One comparison source explicitly mentions combining top-down benchmarks per capita derived from the capacity of the global ecosystem with bottom-up reference data [N4-R1]. This mirrors the broader idea that top-down benchmarks provide the overarching frame or target, while bottom-up benchmarks provide the detailed, site-specific validation and comparison [N4-R1][N9]. In building practice, this might mean using a top-down policy standard as the reference for benchmarking and then using bottom-up data to refine the benchmark, assess compliance, and identify performance gaps [N10][N5-F1]. The combined approach can therefore improve accuracy by reducing the risk of overgeneralization while preserving policy relevance [N4-R5][N12].

External benchmark values are established in building environmental assessments as reference points that allow a building’s performance to be compared with a standard, policy target, or peer group. In practice, they help evaluate whether a building is performing efficiently, whether it meets regulatory or sustainability expectations, and whether improvements are needed [N8]. The purpose of benchmarks is not just to measure; they also support decision-making by providing a common frame for judging energy use, emissions, and operational efficiency [N8]. In building contexts, benchmarking often involves measuring a building’s energy use and comparing it to similar buildings, its own historical usage, or a reference performance level [N5-F1]. This makes external benchmark values central to transparency, compliance, and continuous improvement [N8].

## 1) How bottom-up approaches establish benchmark values

Bottom-up approaches start with detailed, site-specific data and then aggregate it into a benchmark estimate. The evidence shows that bottom-up methods can use building-level or element-level data rather than relying only on external standards as the starting point [N9]. In building assessments, this means using utility energy consumption records, historical usage patterns, and reference performance levels to build a benchmark [N9][N5-F1]. A specific example cited in the branch reports is that bottom-up benchmarks for building elements are calculated following a best-in-class (top 5%) approach, and that a workflow applies these benchmarks [N2-R3]. Another source indicates that benchmarks and/or target values can follow a top-down or bottom-up approach, with the procedure based on best practices [N2-R5].

Inputs are aggregated into benchmark estimates by summarizing detailed local data and comparing it against a comparable reference group or standard. In building benchmarking, this typically means measuring a building’s energy use and then comparing it to similar buildings or a reference performance level [N5-F1]. The bottom-up workflow described in the design-process paper similarly uses detailed building-element data to calculate benchmarks [N2-R3]. The main limitation of this approach is that it depends heavily on the availability, quality, and representativeness of the site-specific data [N9]. It also assumes that the selected reference group is sufficiently comparable to the subject being assessed; otherwise, the comparison may be misleading [N9]. Bottom-up benchmarking can be more sensitive to measurement error and less generalizable than top-down methods [N9]. A further assumption is that a small subset of high-performing examples can inform a broader target, which may not always be defensible without additional validation [N2-R3].

## 2) How top-down approaches establish benchmark values

Top-down approaches derive benchmark values from external datasets, regulatory standards, or broad policy targets rather than from detailed site-specific data. The evidence indicates that top-down benchmarks can be defined based on political or regulatory targets, such as the 2-degree target defined in the Paris Agreement in 2015 [N10]. This means that top-down benchmarks are often framed by broader environmental or policy goals, which then become the reference point for assessing performance [N10]. The branch reports also mention that top-down approaches can be used to assess environmental flows in Australian rivers, showing that benchmarks can be established using flow records or regulatory water-quality standards [N10].

Benchmarks are derived from external data by applying a standard or target to a subject. In the top-down flow-assessment example, the methodology is described as a “top-down” approach for assessing environmental flows, suggesting that a predefined standard or regulatory threshold is applied to determine acceptable environmental conditions [N10]. In building practice, benchmarking is often linked to building performance standards and to policies aimed at reducing energy use and GHG emissions [N5-F1]. This means that top-down benchmarks can be derived by mapping a policy standard onto a building’s performance [N10][N5-F1]. The main limitation of this approach is that it may be less sensitive to site-specific conditions and more susceptible to policy or regulatory shifts [N10]. It also depends on the availability and relevance of the external data source; if the standard is outdated or not well aligned with local conditions, the benchmark may lack practical utility [N10].

## 3) How the two approaches compare and can be combined

The two approaches differ fundamentally in starting point and scope. Bottom-up methods begin with detailed local data and aggregate it into a benchmark estimate, while top-down methods derive benchmarks from external standards, policy targets, or broad datasets [N4-R4][N4-R1]. A key similarity is that both approaches aim to establish a reference against which performance can be measured [N8]. They also both rely on validation and data quality checks in practice [N12].

The main differences are that bottom-up methods are more site-specific and data-intensive, while top-down methods are more policy-aligned and broader in scope [N9][N10]. The comparison source notes that bottom-up estimates account for every known source and a best-guess estimate for each, whereas top-down approaches can be heavily dependent on dataset quality and may differ substantially from bottom-up results [N4-R5]. This means that bottom-up benchmarks can be more accurate for a specific project or building, while top-down benchmarks can be more efficient for setting directionality and aligning with broader sustainability goals [N4-R5][N10].

The approaches can be reconciled or combined by integrating the strengths of each. One comparison source explicitly mentions combining top-down benchmarks per capita derived from the capacity of the global ecosystem with bottom-up reference data [N4-R1]. This mirrors the broader idea that top-down benchmarks provide the overarching frame or target, while bottom-up benchmarks provide the detailed, site-specific validation and comparison [N4-R1][N9]. In building practice, this might mean using a top-down policy standard as the reference for benchmarking and then using bottom-up data to refine the benchmark, assess compliance, and identify performance gaps [N10][N5-F1]. The combined approach can therefore improve accuracy by reducing the risk of overgeneralization while preserving policy relevance [N4-R5][N12].

## 4) Practical validation, reporting, and application

Benchmark values are validated and applied through a combination of data quality checks, statistical verification, and policy alignment. The EPA’s Benchmarking and Building Performance Standards Policy Toolkit emphasizes that improved building performance depends on accurate energy data and that utilities play a critical role in providing whole-building energy consumption data to enable compliance with benchmarking and transparency policies [N12]. This means validation begins with ensuring data access and quality [N12]. The toolkit also explains that benchmarking is used to track GHG emissions and energy, water, and waste costs, suggesting that benchmark values are validated by repeated measurement and comparison across time and buildings [N5-F1][N7-R4].

Validation methods for benchmark accuracy include checking data completeness, consistency, and representativeness [N12]. The benchmark dose guidance also supports this by providing guidance on applying benchmark methods and determining the point of departure for health effects data [N5-R2]. Although this is health risk assessment rather than building benchmarking, it shows that benchmark methods are often supported by technical guidance that defines acceptable statistical procedures and uncertainty ranges [N5-R2]. The broader benchmarking literature also indicates that quantitative and qualitative indicators are identified and verified in environmental impact assessment, and that criteria are developed and applied [N6-R2]. This suggests that benchmark validation may involve indicator selection, verification, and application checks [N6-R2].

Benchmark values are reported and interpreted as performance indicators relative to a reference level. The EPA toolkit states that benchmarking refers to measuring a building’s energy use and comparing it to the energy use of similar buildings, its own historical usage, or a reference performance level [N5-F1]. It also explains that ENERGY STAR scores indicate a building’s energy performance and that benchmarking helps identify performance metrics [N5-F1][N7-R4]. This means that benchmark values are typically reported as scores, intensity ratios, or relative rankings, and are interpreted as indicators of efficiency, compliance, or improvement potential [N5-F1][N7-R4]. The toolkit further notes that benchmarking can be used in transparency policies, building performance standards, and energy audits, showing that benchmark values are interpreted in policy and compliance contexts rather than as standalone scientific metrics [N5-F1].

Use cases and decision-support roles are widespread. In buildings, benchmarking supports energy reduction, GHG emission reduction, energy cost savings, increased building asset values, local job creation, indoor air quality improvements, tenant comfort, and reduced power plant emissions [N5-F1]. In environmental assessments, benchmark methodology is used to assess impacts by objective considerations and to conduct comparisons [N1-R2]. The benchmark dose guidance also supports risk assessment by helping determine the point of departure for health effects data [N5-R2]. Taken together, benchmark values serve decision-making roles such as setting targets, evaluating performance, enforcing standards, and identifying areas for improvement [N1-R2][N5-F1][N5-R2].

## 5) Bottom line: when each approach is preferred

Bottom-up approaches are especially useful when detailed local data are available and when the goal is to derive performance-specific benchmarks for individual buildings or building elements [N9]. They are well suited to benchmarking, energy audits, retrocommissioning, and building performance standards because they can map to actual usage patterns and historical benchmarks [N5-F1]. Top-down approaches are preferred when there is a strong external standard, policy target, or regulatory benchmark, such as climate targets, water-quality thresholds, or building-performance requirements [N10][N3-R1]. They are especially useful for setting directionality, enforcing compliance, and aligning projects with broader sustainability goals [N8][N10].

## 6) Integrated conclusion

In building environmental assessments, external benchmark values are established by comparing a building’s performance to a reference standard, peer group, or policy target. Bottom-up approaches start with detailed local data and aggregate it into a benchmark estimate, while top-down approaches derive benchmarks from external datasets, regulatory standards, or broad policy targets [N4-R4][N4-R1][N10]. Bottom-up methods are more site-specific and data-intensive, while top-down methods are more policy-aligned and broader in scope [N9][N10]. Both approaches are validated through data quality checks, statistical verification, and policy alignment, and both are reported as performance indicators relative to a reference level [N12][N5-F1].

The most useful practice is often to combine the two approaches: use top-down benchmarks to set the overarching target or standard, and use bottom-up data to refine the benchmark, assess compliance, and identify performance gaps [N4-R1][N10][N9]. This combination improves accuracy, reduces overgeneralization, and preserves the practical relevance of benchmarking [N4-R5][N12].

External benchmark values are comparison points used in environmental assessments to evaluate how a project, building, or activity performs relative to a standard or reference level. In practice, they help decision-makers judge whether a proposed action is environmentally acceptable, efficient, or aligned with broader sustainability goals [N1-R2]. The EPA’s Benchmarking and Building Performance Standards Policy Toolkit explains that benchmarking refers to measuring a building’s energy use and comparing it to the energy use of similar buildings, its own historical usage, or a reference performance level [N5-F1]. This is a core practical example of how benchmark values are established: by linking a subject to a comparable external standard or baseline [N5-F1].

The attributes typically benchmarked in environmental assessments depend on the context, but building-related benchmarks often focus on energy use, water use, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. The EPA toolkit states that many state and local governments couple benchmarking policies with other programs aimed at encouraging building performance, including voluntary campaigns, energy audits, retrocommissioning, and building performance standards. It also notes that energy use of buildings is a key first step to understanding and improving energy performance and reducing carbon footprints [N5-F1]. The toolkit further mentions GHG emissions and energy, water, and waste costs as tracked metrics [N7-R4]. This indicates that external benchmarks commonly cover energy intensity, emissions intensity, and operational resource use, especially in buildings [N5-F1][N7-R4].

Benchmarks matter because they support comparison and decision-making. The benchmark methodology described in the environmental impact assessment literature makes it possible to assess impacts by objective considerations and to conduct comparisons [N1-R2]. In buildings, benchmarking helps governments and jurisdictions identify performance metrics and establish policies that drive energy savings and emissions reductions [N5-F1]. The toolkit also highlights that improved performance in existing buildings can help achieve decarbonization goals and deliver benefits such as energy cost savings, increased building asset values, local job creation, indoor air quality improvements, tenant comfort, productivity, and reduced power plant emissions [N5-F1]. In short, benchmark values turn abstract environmental goals into actionable targets by providing a common reference against which performance can be judged [N1-R2][N5-F1].

Bottom-up approaches generate benchmark values by starting with detailed, site-specific data and aggregating it into a broader estimate. The evidence suggests that bottom-up methods use building-level or element-level data rather than relying on external standards as the starting point. One source notes that bottom-up benchmarks for building elements are calculated following a best-in-class (top 5%) approach, and that a workflow applies these benchmarks [N2-R3]. Another source in the search results refers to generating benchmarks and/or target values based on best practices, with the procedure following a top-down or bottom-up approach [N2-R5]. While this latter excerpt is not fully quoted, it is relevant because it shows that bottom-up benchmarking is positioned as a method of deriving target values from practice-based criteria rather than from a single external standard [N2-R5].

The data sources used in bottom-up methods are typically operational and granular. In building assessments, the EPA toolkit explains that benchmarking is based on measuring a building’s energy use and comparing it to similar buildings, its own historical usage, or a reference performance level [N5-F1]. This implies that bottom-up benchmarking may draw from utility data, energy consumption records, historical usage patterns, and building-specific metrics such as ENERGY STAR scores [N5-F1][N7-R4]. The benchmark dose literature also indicates that benchmark methods can be applied using quantitative and qualitative indicators, with criteria developed for environmental impact assessment [N6-R2]. This reinforces that bottom-up benchmarking is not purely statistical; it often includes indicator selection, verification, and application [N6-R2].

Inputs are aggregated into benchmark estimates by summarizing site-specific data and comparing it against a reference or peer group. In the building context, benchmarking is described as measuring energy use and then comparing it to similar buildings, which effectively aggregates individual building data into a benchmark-level comparison [N5-F1]. The bottom-up workflow described in the design-process paper similarly suggests that detailed building-element data are used to calculate benchmarks [N2-R3]. However, this approach depends on assumptions that the selected data are representative of the population or target group being compared, that the aggregation is statistically valid, and that the chosen reference group is comparable [N2-R3][N2-R5].

Bottom-up benchmarking has several limitations and assumptions. First, it can be data-intensive and dependent on the availability and quality of site-specific records [N5-F1]. Second, it assumes that the benchmark reference group is sufficiently comparable to the subject being assessed; otherwise, the comparison may be misleading [N5-F1][N2-R3]. Third, because it starts with detailed local data, it may be more sensitive to measurement error and less generalizable than top-down methods [N2-R3]. Finally, the use of best-in-class approaches implies an assumption that a small subset of high-performing examples can inform a broader target, which may not always be defensible without additional validation [N2-R3].

Top-down approaches establish benchmark values by deriving them from external datasets, regulatory standards, or broad policy targets rather than from detailed site-specific data. The evidence indicates that top-down benchmarks can be defined based on political or regulatory targets. One source explicitly states that top-down benchmarks are typically defined based on a political target, such as the 2-degree target defined in the Paris Agreement in 2015 [N3-R1]. This shows that top-down benchmarks are often framed by broader environmental or policy goals, which then become the reference point for assessing performance [N3-R1].

The reference datasets or regulatory standards used in top-down benchmarking include environmental regulations, climate targets, and policy frameworks. The Paris Agreement’s 2-degree target is an example of a regulatory-standard-like benchmark that sets an upper limit for temperature rise [N3-R1]. The benchmarking literature also describes a top-down methodology for assessing environmental flows in Australian rivers, which implies that hydrological benchmarks can be established using flow records or regulatory water-quality standards [N3-R2]. In building and energy contexts, the EPA toolkit notes that benchmarking is often linked to building performance standards and that state and local governments may adopt policies aimed at reducing energy use and GHG emissions [N5-F1]. These policies and standards themselves function as external references for benchmarking [N5-F1].

Benchmarks are derived from external data by applying a standard or target to a subject. In the top-down flow-assessment example, the methodology is described as a “top-down” approach for assessing environmental flows, suggesting that a predefined standard or regulatory threshold is applied to determine acceptable environmental conditions [N3-R2]. The Paris Agreement example shows that a global climate target can become the basis for sectoral or project-level benchmarks [N3-R1]. In building performance, benchmarking often compares a building’s energy use to a reference performance level, which may be derived from a standard, policy requirement, or average benchmark [N5-F1]. This means that top-down benchmarks are usually derived by mapping external standards or targets onto the subject’s performance [N3-R1][N3-R2][N5-F1].

Top-down benchmarking has its own limitations and assumptions. One limitation is that it may be less sensitive to site-specific conditions and more susceptible to policy or regulatory shifts [N3-R1]. Another assumption is that the external standard is both meaningful and comparable to the subject being assessed; otherwise, the benchmark may not reflect actual environmental or operational realities [N3-R2][N5-F1]. The methodology also depends on the availability and relevance of the external data source; if the standard is outdated or not well aligned with local conditions, the benchmark may lack practical utility [N3-R1][N3-R2]. Overall, top-down benchmarking is efficient and policy-aligned, but it risks being too generic or detached from local performance details [N3-R1][N3-R2].

Bottom-up and top-down approaches differ fundamentally in their starting point and scope. Bottom-up methods begin with detailed, local data and aggregate it into a benchmark estimate, while top-down methods derive benchmarks from external standards, policy targets, or broad datasets [N4-R4][N4-R1]. In building environmental assessments, bottom-up approaches often use building-level or element-level data, including utility energy consumption records, historical usage, and reference performance levels [N9]. Top-down approaches, by contrast, may be defined by political targets such as the 2-degree Paris Agreement target or by regulatory standards and flow thresholds [N10].

A key similarity is that both approaches aim to establish a reference against which performance can be measured. The upstream reports show that benchmark values support comparison and decision-making by providing a common standard for judging energy use, emissions, and operational efficiency [N8]. They also both rely on validation and data quality checks in practice [N12]. A difference is that bottom-up methods are more site-specific and data-intensive, while top-down methods are more policy-aligned and broader in scope [N9][N10]. The comparison source also notes that bottom-up estimates account for every known source and a best-guess estimate for each, whereas top-down approaches can be heavily dependent on dataset quality and may differ substantially from bottom-up results [N4-R5].

Each approach is preferred depending on the context. Bottom-up methods are especially useful when detailed local data are available and when the goal is to derive performance-specific benchmarks for individual buildings or building elements [N9]. They are well suited to benchmarking, energy audits, retrocommissioning, and building performance standards because they can map to actual usage patterns and historical benchmarks [N5-F1]. Top-down methods are preferred when there is a strong external standard, policy target, or regulatory benchmark, such as climate targets, water-quality thresholds, or building-performance requirements [N10][N3-R1]. They are especially useful for setting directionality, enforcing compliance, and aligning projects with broader sustainability goals [N8][N10].

The approaches can be reconciled or combined by integrating the strengths of each. One comparison source explicitly mentions combining top-down benchmarks per capita derived from the capacity of the global ecosystem with bottom-up reference data [N4-R1]. This mirrors the broader idea that top-down benchmarks provide the overarching frame or target, while bottom-up benchmarks provide the detailed, site-specific validation and comparison [N4-R1][N9]. In building practice, this might mean using a top-down policy standard as the reference for benchmarking and then using bottom-up data to refine the benchmark, assess compliance, and identify performance gaps [N10][N5-F1]. The combined approach can therefore improve accuracy by reducing the risk of overgeneralization while preserving policy relevance [N4-R5][N12].

In practice, they help evaluate whether a building is performing efficiently, whether it meets regulatory or sustainability expectations, and whether improvements are needed [N8]. The purpose of benchmarks is not just to measure; they also support decision-making by providing a common frame for judging energy use, emissions, and operational efficiency [N8]. In building contexts, benchmarking often involves measuring a building’s energy use and comparing it to similar buildings, its own historical usage, or a reference performance level [N5-F1]. This makes external benchmark values central to transparency, compliance, and continuous improvement [N8].

## 1) How bottom-up approaches establish benchmark values

Bottom-up approaches start with detailed, site-specific data and then aggregate it into a benchmark estimate. The evidence shows that bottom-up methods can use building-level or element-level data rather than relying only on external standards as the starting point [N9]. In building assessments, this means using utility energy consumption records, historical usage patterns, and reference performance levels to build a benchmark [N9][N5-F1]. A specific example cited in the branch reports is that bottom-up benchmarks for building elements are calculated following a best-in-class (top 5%) approach, and that a workflow applies these benchmarks [N2-R3]. Another source indicates that benchmarks and/or target values can follow a top-down or bottom-up approach, with the procedure based on best practices [N2-R5].

Inputs are aggregated into benchmark estimates by summarizing detailed local data and comparing it against a comparable reference group or standard. In building benchmarking, this typically means measuring a building’s energy use and then comparing it to similar buildings or a reference performance level [N5-F1]. The bottom-up workflow described in the design-process paper similarly uses detailed building-element data to calculate benchmarks [N2-R3]. The main limitation of this approach is that it depends heavily on the availability, quality, and representativeness of the site-specific data [N9]. It also assumes that the selected reference group is sufficiently comparable to the subject being assessed; otherwise, the comparison may be misleading [N9]. Bottom-up benchmarking can be more sensitive to measurement error and less generalizable than top-down methods [N9]. A further assumption is that a small subset of high-performing examples can inform a broader target, which may not always be defensible without additional validation [N2-R3].

## 2) How top-down approaches establish benchmark values

Top-down approaches derive benchmark values from external datasets, regulatory standards, or broad policy targets rather than from detailed site-specific data. The evidence indicates that top-down benchmarks can be defined based on political or regulatory targets, such as the 2-degree target defined in the Paris Agreement in 2015 [N10]. This means that top-down benchmarks are often framed by broader environmental or policy goals, which then become the reference point for assessing performance [N10]. The branch reports also mention that top-down approaches can be used to assess environmental flows in Australian rivers, showing that benchmarks can be established using flow records or regulatory water-quality standards [N10].

Benchmarks are derived from external data by applying a standard or target to a subject. In the top-down flow-assessment example, the methodology is described as a “top-down” approach for assessing environmental flows, suggesting that a predefined standard or regulatory threshold is applied to determine acceptable environmental conditions [N10]. In building practice, benchmarking is often linked to building performance standards and to policies aimed at reducing energy use and GHG emissions [N5-F1]. This means that top-down benchmarks can be derived by mapping a policy standard onto a building’s performance [N10][N5-F1]. The main limitation of this approach is that it may be less sensitive to site-specific conditions and more susceptible to policy or regulatory shifts [N10]. It also depends on the availability and relevance of the external data source; if the standard is outdated or not well aligned with local conditions, the benchmark may lack practical utility [N10].

## 3) How the two approaches compare and can be combined

The two approaches differ fundamentally in starting point and scope. Bottom-up methods begin with detailed local data and aggregate it into a benchmark estimate, while top-down methods derive benchmarks from external standards, policy targets, or broad datasets [N4-R4][N4-R1]. A key similarity is that both approaches aim to establish a reference against which performance can be measured [N8]. They also both rely on validation and data quality checks in practice [N12].

The main differences are that bottom-up methods are more site-specific and data-intensive, while top-down methods are more policy-aligned and broader in scope [N9][N10]. The comparison source notes that bottom-up estimates account for every known source and a best-guess estimate for each, whereas top-down approaches can be heavily dependent on dataset quality and may differ substantially from bottom-up results [N4-R5]. This means that bottom-up benchmarks can be more accurate for a specific project or building, while top-down benchmarks can be more efficient for setting directionality and aligning with broader sustainability goals [N4-R5][N10].

## 6) Integrated conclusion

In building environmental assessments, external benchmark values are established by comparing a building’s performance to a reference standard, peer group, or policy target. Bottom-up approaches start with detailed local data and aggregate it into a benchmark estimate, while top-down approaches derive benchmarks from external datasets, regulatory standards, or broad policy targets [N4-R4][N4-R1][N10]. Bottom-up and top-down approaches differ fundamentally in their starting point and scope. Bottom-up methods begin with detailed, local data and aggregate it into a benchmark estimate, while top-down methods derive benchmarks from external standards, policy targets, or broad datasets [N4-R4][N4-R1]. In building environmental assessments, bottom-up approaches often use building-level or element-level data, including utility energy consumption records, historical usage, and reference performance levels [N9]. Top-down approaches, by contrast, may be defined by political targets such as the 2-degree Paris Agreement target or by regulatory standards and flow thresholds [N10].

A key similarity is that both approaches aim to establish a reference against which performance can be measured. The upstream reports show that benchmark values support comparison and decision-making by providing a common standard for judging energy use, emissions, and operational efficiency [N8]. They also both rely on validation and data quality checks in practice [N12]. A difference is that bottom-up methods are more site-specific and data-intensive, while top-down methods are more policy-aligned and broader in scope [N9][N10]. Top-down methods are preferred when there is a strong external standard, policy target, or regulatory benchmark, such as climate targets, water-quality thresholds, or building-performance requirements [N10][N3-R1]. They are especially useful for setting directionality, enforcing compliance, and aligning projects with broader sustainability goals [N8][N10].

One comparison source explicitly mentions combining top-down benchmarks per capita derived from the capacity of the global ecosystem with bottom-up reference data [N4-R1]. This mirrors the broader idea that top-down benchmarks provide the overarching frame or target, while bottom-up benchmarks provide the detailed, site-specific validation and comparison [N4-R1][N9]. The combined approach can therefore improve accuracy by reducing the risk of overgeneralization while preserving policy relevance [N4-R5][N12].

Top-down approaches derive benchmark values from external datasets, regulatory standards, or broad policy targets rather than from detailed site-specific data.
